To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
a healthy adult male, with a persisting monoclonal T cell population in the peripheral blood, has been identified.
a normal adult male had an expansion of CD8+ TCR Vα 12+ Vβ 52+ T cells, and that this expansion was monoclonal, as determined by Vβ‐PCR and Jβ‐PCR.

a normal healthy adult male was shown to harbour an expanded T cell population, which persisted over the observation time of more than one year, and was found to be monoclonally expanded by PCR‐analysis.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the discovery and characterization of a novel T cell expansion in an otherwise healthy individual.
the identification and characterization of a novel clinical entity.
the identification of a new clinical entity of a persistent T cell expansion, which may represent the earliest stage of T cell lymphoproliferative disorder.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
MTUS constitutes a new clinical entity.
this condition represents a new clinical entity.
the expanded T cell population was monoclonal, non‐activated and of virgin cell type.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

a persistent, monoclonal T cell population, expressing TCR containing the Vα 1.2.1 and Vβ 5,2 gene segments, is present in the peripheral blood and lymphoid tissues of a healthy adult male, and that this condition is designated ‘monoclanal T cell expansion’.
MTUS represents the expansion of a single, presumably self‐reactive, T cell clone which has not yet undergone malignant transformation.
the expanded T cells in MTUS were of ‘virgin cell type’ and were non‐activated and non‐malignant, and that they were monoclonal and clonal in nature.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the condition is not rare and may be more frequent than previously assumed.
the expanded T cells are not only of ‘virgin’, non‐activated type, but they also appear to be monoclonally derived.
a persistent monoclonal T cell proliferation may be present in a healthy adult, without causing any clinical symptoms.
